comments.author: @Peanuts001-y5o
comments.text: I went to Mauritius in 1978, from France with a friend, no plans. At the airport, there were people offering rentals, extremely friendly French speaking family rented us a Bungalow for 10 days. In those days it was expensive, but very beautiful and wild. There wasn't a big city with high rises, yes many hotels on the water. Lots of pick pockets at the market and quite segregated between the local Hindu population and those of French origin. I barely recognize Mauritius in this film.

replies.author: @RemoteEarthJourneys
replies.text: Exactly! 🌊 In Mauritius, the ocean isn’t just something beautiful to look at—it shapes work, food, transport, weather, and even the rhythm of daily life. That quiet beauty hits differently once you realize how deeply the island’s people are connected to it. 🌴

comments.author: @EarthinMotion25
comments.text: The ability of the population to switch effortlessly between Creole at home, English in schools, and French in the news is a remarkable testament to human integration. It is a practical survival skill that has evolved into a unique cultural identity.

replies.author: @chesn00
replies.text: @WorldDiscovered_Official These three languages are the basis of Mauritian culture, everyone understands and can speak. In face we have an over 80% literate population. Aside from English, French, and Creole, there are oriental languages carried down from ancestors that are still spoken and learned in schools, for example, Bhojpuri, Hindi, Urdu, Arabic, Mandarin, Tamil, Telugu

replies.author: @WorldDiscovered_Official
replies.text: Do most young Mauritians feel equally comfortable speaking Creole, English, and French, or is one language becoming more dominant among the younger generation?

replies.author: @RemoteEarthJourneys
replies.text: Absolutely! That linguistic flexibility feels like one of Mauritius’s greatest strengths. Three languages before lunch, several cultures before dinner, and somehow the conversation still ends with curry! 😂 It’s more than communication—it’s a living piece of the island’s history and identity.
